title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
content_html:
Exam Format Overview

The War of the Worlds question will appear on your 19th-century literature paper. It tests AO1 (response with textual references), AO2 (analysis of methods and effects) and AO3 (context). This is typically a closed-text exam. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact format, mark weightings and timing.

You may face an extract-based question (analyse a given passage, then extend to the whole novel) or a discursive question (no extract; choose your own evidence). Both require clear argument, embedded quotations, and woven Assessment Objectives.

Key Fact

AO1 = response with textual references. AO2 = analysis of Wells’s methods and effects. AO3 = understanding of Victorian context (imperialism, evolution, class). All three must be woven together, not treated as separate sections.

Structuring an Analytical Response

Use the WHAT-HOW-WHY model: WHAT (state your point, AO1), HOW (analyse Wells’s method with a quotation, AO2), WHY (embed context, AO3). For Wells, key methods include: first-person narration, scientific register, imperial analogy, documentary realism, the anti-climactic ending.

Aim for 4–5 analytical paragraphs within the time allowed. Begin with a clear thesis and end with a brief conclusion linking back to your opening argument.

Imperialism: “Before we judge them too harshly...” — narrator’s direct comparison. Technology: “a monstrous tripod, higher than many houses” — scale of threat. Human response: “By ten o’clock the police organisation was lost in the growing pressure of the flight” — civilisation’s collapse. Resolution: “slain by the humblest things” — ironic defeat.

Key Quotations to Memorise

Imperialism: “Before we judge them too harshly, we must remember what ruthless and utter destruction our own species has wrought.” Technology: “an almost noiseless and blinding flash of light” (Heat-Ray). Evolution: “slain by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this earth” (bacteria). Civilisation: “never before in the history of the world had such a mass of human beings moved and suffered together.”

Retelling the plot: the examiner knows the story. Every sentence should analyse, not narrate. Ignoring AO3: Wells wrote this novel specifically to critique imperialism — context is essential. Treating the novel as just an adventure story: always link events to Wells’s social purpose.

Key Fact

Memorise short quotations per theme: imperialism (“ruthless and utter destruction our own species has wrought”), technology (the Heat-Ray), evolution (bacteria), civilisation’s collapse (the London exodus). Practise embedding them in analytical sentences.
exam_tip_html: For The War of the Worlds, always link events to Wells’s critique of imperialism (AO3). The examiner rewards responses that treat the novel as social commentary, not just adventure. For AO2, focus on Wells’s methods: first-person narration, scientific register, documentary realism.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Reverse imperialism forces Victorians to confront their role as colonisers.
  • Wells draws on Darwin to question human superiority and civilisation’s permanence.
  • For OCR, embed context within analysis. Both question types are worth 40 marks.
